title: Access Methods
lead: Find the names of 20-year-old students on four stored pages. Then see exactly what an index can skip, what it still must read, and when it adds work.
goals: Distinguish sequential-scan cost from output selectivity
Check whether an index can support a predicate in key order
Apply the equality-prefix/range rule to a composite B+ tree
Compare index-only, clustered, and unclustered scans

sections.title: Find one student, then account for every page
sections.html:
Ask one concrete question: SELECT name FROM Students WHERE age=20. The table is stored on four pages, with three rows on each. These are original teaching data, not a table copied from the slides. Assume pages are not already cached and the query asks for every match.

PageSlot 1Slot 2Slot 3
P1An, 19Bình, 40Chi, 27
P2Dũng, 22Giang, 35Hạnh, 24
P3Khoa, 31Linh, 20Minh, 29
P4Nam, 45Oanh, 23Phúc, 26

Without another structure, read P1 and test its three ages: no match. Read P2: no match. Read P3: Linh matches. We can emit Linh now, but cannot stop: P4 could contain another 20-year-old. Read P4, find none, and finish. The answer has one name; finding all names cost four data-page reads. This way of visiting each table page and checking its rows is a sequential scan.

Now add a separate age index that stores pairs of age and record location. Its entry 20 → (P3, slot 2) tells us where to look. That location is a record identifier (RID). It is not the name Linh. After finding the index entry, fetch P3 and read slot 2 to obtain the requested name. An index scan therefore has separate work: find index entries, then fetch required table data.

How do we find age 20 without reading the whole index? A B+ tree arranges entries in sorted leaves and uses higher-level guide pages to route toward the appropriate leaf. That descent has a cost. If an illustrative uncached tree needs two internal reads, one leaf read, and the P3 fetch, this tiny lookup costs four page reads too. A large table may offer much larger savings; “has an index” does not mean “free lookup.”

Change the question before claiming the index wins

For age>=19, all 12 rows qualify. The index cannot let us skip any table page when names are required, and it adds index traversal/scanning work. A sequential scan can be preferable. For ages 20 through 24, sorted entries are 20→P3, 22→P2, 23→P4, 24→P2. They are adjacent in age order but visit data pages in the order P3/P2/P4/P2. Index order is different from physical row placement; keeping P2 cached may avoid its second disk read.

An access method is one of these concrete ways to retrieve rows. The optimizer compares applicable methods and chooses a plan using estimated cost. The access method performs the retrieval; it does not itself establish that it was the cheapest candidate.

Why does finding RID (P3, slot 2) not yet answer SELECT name?

The age index contains age and location, not name. Fetching that table slot supplies Linh. Changing the output to age could remove that fetch if everything needed is in the index; we develop that case below.

Key takeaway

Distinguish pages read from pages remaining after filtering. Low selectivity produces a small output, but a sequential scan still reads the whole table unless some mechanism lets it skip pages.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 2–6.

sections.title: A second index column is ordered within the first
sections.html:
An age-only index cannot directly narrow a query by department. Add an index on (department,age,salary). The column order matters: all CS entries are together; within CS they are ordered by age; only within equal ages are they ordered by salary. This is lexicographic order, like sorting names by surname and then given name.

Use this original leaf sequence:

(CS,22,500) (CS,31,400) (CS,31,500)
(CS,35,300) (CS,35,500) (EE,22,500)

For department=CS AND age>30, find the first CS entry above age 30, then scan until the CS group ends: four entries. For department=CS AND age=31 AND salary>450, fix department and age, then scan the salary suffix: only (CS,31,500). Both predicates describe one contiguous interval.

Now ask department=CS AND age>30 AND salary=500. The same four age-range candidates must be considered. Test salary on them: reject (31,400), keep (31,500), reject (35,300), keep (35,500). Salary=500 does not form one uninterrupted interval after an age range. It is a residual condition: still checked, but not sufficient to shrink this range into just its two answers.

The general rule for this teaching model follows from that order: bind zero or more leading columns by equality, then at most the next column by a range. A lookup for age=31 without department is not a leading-prefix lookup here. Specialized skip-scan techniques are outside this model; do not assume that a missing prefix makes every possible full index scan impossible.

Hashing solves a different lookup problem

A hash index on (department,age) computes a bucket from the complete pair. CS and 31 together select a bucket; CS alone or age>30 does not. Hashing does not preserve neighboring ages as neighboring entries.

Once in a bucket, still compare the actual key: different keys can share a bucket. If keys are nonunique, finding one match cannot justify stopping, because more matches may be in overflow pages. A bucket with one primary page and two overflow pages requires three bucket-page reads for a complete nonunique lookup. Directory lookup and table fetches are additional costs. With a known unique key, a successful search can stop when that unique match is found; an unsuccessful search must establish absence.

Which is a single range in (A,B): A=7 AND B>20, or A>7 AND B=20?

The first fixes A and scans within its B order. The second scans several A groups and tests B inside each; those B=20 answers are separated by other B values.

Key takeaway

Read a composite key from left to right. In this B+ tree model, fix the leading columns with equality conditions, then use one range. Conditions on later columns may still require additional checks.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 7–15; Source PDF · physical pages 19; physical PDF page 19.

sections.title: Avoid a table fetch only when the index contains the answer
sections.html:
Return to the Students age index. SELECT age ... WHERE age=20 needs only a stored search key, whereas SELECT name needs P3. An index-only plan uses index contents for every required output and test. In the slide teaching model it avoids data-page fetches. Real systems can still need visibility checks, so physical behavior depends on the DBMS.

The same idea supports aggregation. An index with one entry per employee on department contains enough values to count employees per department. An ordered index on (department,salary) groups salaries by department and supports reasoning about each department's minimum. An age/salary index can supply both the age filter and salaries for AVG when the query needs no missing column. Correct counts still require retaining each row's multiplicity.

When table fetches remain, physical placement matters. A clustered index puts nearby keys on nearby data pages; an unclustered one can scatter them as P3/P2/P4/P2. To group repeated page visits, collect RIDs and order them by page. For [7,2,7,4,2], page grouping visits 2,4,7, just three distinct pages if retained during this phase. It changes access order, not the five matching rows.

In the earlier index-storage terminology, variant A stores complete records as data entries, while variants B/C use keys with RIDs (one RID or a RID list). Our age example uses the key-and-location model. Whether the leaf itself contains name is what decides whether SELECT name needs another fetch.

Keep traversal, leaf scanning and table reads separate

Let h count internal-node reads before the first leaf, L be all leaf pages, N all data pages, and s the fraction of index entries in the candidate contiguous range. Assume uniform entry density. Leaf scanning is approximately sL. If all candidates are fetched and clustered on fraction s of data pages, fetch work is sN.

Candidate, under these assumptionsFormulah=3, L=120, N=900, s=0.05
Clustered, needs table columnsh+sL+sN3+6+45=54
Index-onlyh+sL3+6=9

h excludes the leaf to avoid counting it twice. If a later salary condition keeps only half the candidates, do not automatically halve sL: the scan still crosses the original age range. If the index evaluates salary before fetching, the data-fetch term may decrease separately. For an unclustered path a pessimistic model charges one data read per fetched tuple, but caching and grouping can reduce it.

Combine locations before fetching rows

Suppose an age index yields RIDs {1,3,6,9} and a department index yields {2,3,6,8}. AND keeps the intersection {3,6}; OR keeps the union {1,2,3,6,8,9}. A bitmap represents candidate row locations and can organize table visits by page. Fetch those candidates, then test country='UK' if neither index established that condition. Combining two index sets did not magically test a third column. Any required recheck still applies.

Does s=0.05 prove that 5% of table pages are fetched?

No. It is a candidate-entry fraction. The sN fetch approximation additionally assumes clustered placement and that the candidate distribution occupies that fraction of pages. An unclustered arrangement can touch much more.

sections.title: Optional experiment: explain the plan you actually receive
sections.html:
First make a prediction from the lesson: does an index help more when 100 out of 10,000 rows qualify, or when all 10,000 qualify? Test it in an existing PostgreSQL session, such as psql connected to a disposable database. This is outside the site's SQLite runner. If PostgreSQL is unavailable, work through the supplied interpretation instead.

CREATE TEMP TABLE adbs_access_demo (
 id integer PRIMARY KEY, age integer NOT NULL, padding text NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO adbs_access_demo
SELECT g, g % 100, repeat('x',100)
FROM generate_series(1,10000) AS generated(g);
CREATE INDEX adbs_access_demo_age_idx ON adbs_access_demo(age);
ANALYZE adbs_access_demo;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, age FROM adbs_access_demo WHERE age=7;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, age FROM adbs_access_demo WHERE age>=0;

The temporary table lasts only for this session. Ages 0 through 99 each occur 100 times. Therefore age=7 returns 100 rows, while age>=0 returns 10,000. ANALYZE collects statistics; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the SELECT and reports measurements beside estimates.

Seq Scan on adbs_access_demo (... rows=100 ...)
  (actual ... rows=100 loops=1)
  Filter: (age = 7)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 9900
  Buffers: local hit=200

This is an illustrative fragment, not a recorded run of the fixture. The first rows=100 is estimated output; actual rows=100 is measured output per loop. The scan tests all rows and rejects 9,900. local hit=200 describes cached temporary-page accesses, not 200 disk reads or a guarantee that the table has 200 pages.

What if both queries get a sequential scan?

Record both outcomes and inspect table size, cache, statistics, and retrieval cost. A plan change is not guaranteed. The useful test is whether you can explain the chosen access work and compare estimated versus actual rows, rather than force a particular scan name.

The official Bike Sharing worksheet and dataset require Learn access and were not accessed. This is a separate original exercise. To finish without PostgreSQL, explain why the Students age RID lacks name, why ages 20–24 revisit P2, and which output change could permit index-only access.

quiz.question: Which predicate forms a contiguous range in an index on (A,B)?
options: B=20 with any value of A
A>7 AND B=20 with no residual check needed at all
quiz.explanation: An equality prefix on A followed by a range on B forms one contiguous interval in the index.
